claims.text: The ability of high-entropy alloys to develop and retain a protective oxide layer is governed by selective oxidation of minor alloying elements.
Selectively oxidized minor alloying elements form a continuous and adherent oxide barrier.
Thermodynamic phase stability and oxidation kinetics enable rapid protective-scale formation under oxidizing conditions.
CALPHAD can predict the phase stability governing the proposed oxidation behavior.
The relevant alloys contain minor concentrations of oxidation-prone species within an otherwise homogeneous multicomponent microstructure.
A continuous, adherent scale such as Al2O3 or Cr2O3 interrupts further oxidation.
The protective oxide scale limits oxidation by blocking oxygen and metal-ion transport.
In an oxidizing atmosphere, elements with higher oxidation affinity selectively oxidize and stabilize the alloy surface.
Under vacuum, insufficient oxygen prevents the proposed selective oxidation and produces a different surface chemistry.
Air-treated samples at 900°C–1100°C will develop a distinct surface oxide phase detectable by HTXRD.
Vacuum-treated samples will exhibit minimal or no oxide-scale formation.
Formation of the protective oxide in air will correlate with enhanced oxidation resistance relative to the vacuum-treated baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies approximately from 900°C to 1100°C when the alloy contains enough protective-oxide-forming minor elements.
The mechanism may fail when protective-oxide-forming elements are absent or when the temperature lies outside 900°C–1100°C.
